executive_summary.title: Executive Summary
executive_summary.content: Proton Exchange Membrane (PEM) electrolyzers are evaluated in techno-economic analyses [cite_exec_cit_2] and face significant material bottlenecks [cite_exec_cit_1]. Standard commercial deployments are bottlenecked by high iridium catalyst loadings at the anode [cite_exec_cit_1]. Addressing these challenges requires innovative catalyst design and cost reduction strategies [cite_exec_cit_1].

claims.text: Proton Exchange Membrane (PEM) electrolyzers face material constraints due to high iridium catalyst loadings, requiring innovative catalyst design and cost reduction.
Techno-economic modeling provides insights into cost requirements and operational lifetimes for Proton Exchange Membrane (PEM) electrolyzers.

sections.title: Catalyst Innovations and Supply Chain Bottlenecks
sections.content: Commercial PEM electrolyzers typically utilize anode iridium catalyst loadings between 1.5 and 2.0 mg/cm^2 [cite_cite_1]. These high loadings create severe supply chain bottlenecks for gigawatt-scale manufacturing [cite_cite_1]. Recent research demonstrates that synthesizing atom-dispersed iridium on conductive antimony-doped tin oxide supports can drastically reduce iridium loading to 0.18 mg/cm^2 while preserving electrochemical performance, achieving a cell voltage of 1.78 V at a current density of 2.0 A/cm^2 [cite_cite_2].

claims.text: Commercial PEM electrolyzers rely on anode iridium catalyst loadings of 1.5 to 2.0 mg/cm^2, causing severe supply chain bottlenecks for gigawatt-scale scaling.
Using atom-dispersed iridium on antimony-doped tin oxide supports reduces iridium loading to 0.18 mg/cm^2 and maintains 1.78 V cell voltage at 2.0 A/cm^2 current density.

citations.quoted_passage: Synthesizing atom-dispersed iridium on conductive antimony-doped tin oxide (ATO) supports enables reducing iridium loading to 0.18 mg/cm^2 while maintaining a cell voltage of 1.78 V at a current density of 2.0 A/cm^2.

sections.title: Techno-Economic Modeling and Operational Durability
sections.content: Techno-economic modeling shows that achieving a levelized cost of hydrogen below $2.00/kg demands an electricity input cost below $0.03/kWh along with stack capital expenditures under $350/kW [cite_cite_3]. Furthermore, high-frequency power transients lead to the acceleration of cerium radical scavenger migration in Nafion membranes, which decreases operational stack lifetime from 80,000 down to 52,000 hours [cite_cite_4].

claims.text: Achieving a levelized cost of hydrogen (LCOH) below $2.00/kg requires electricity input costs below $0.03/kWh and stack capital expenditures under $350/kW.
High-frequency power transients accelerate cerium radical scavenger migration in Nafion membranes, cutting stack operational lifetime from 80,000 to 52,000 hours.

citations.quoted_passage: High-frequency power transients accelerate cerium radical scavenger migration in Nafion membranes, reducing operational stack lifetime from 80,000 to 52,000 hours.

conclusion.title: Conclusion and Future Outlook
conclusion.content: Overcoming material hurdles in PEM electrolysis depends on successfully scaling catalyst innovations like atom-dispersed iridium on ATO supports to alleviate material scarcity [cite_conc_cit_1]. Additionally, high-frequency power transients affect membrane durability by accelerating cerium radical scavenger migration, which reduces operational stack lifetime [cite_conc_cit_2].

claims.text: Overcoming production hurdles requires scaling atom-dispersed iridium on ATO supports to alleviate material scarcity.
High-frequency power transients reduce operational stack lifetime by accelerating cerium radical scavenger migration in Nafion membranes.

limitations: The analysis relies on limited context regarding specific manufacturing yields for atom-dispersed iridium catalysts at industrial scales.
Data regarding off-grid power transient mitigation strategies for Nafion membranes remains restricted.
